[[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]] — what's left, and how to talk about this work externally\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/01 - What is CausalOps (Project Primer).md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: reference\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, project-primer, onboarding]\n---\n\n# What is CausalOps? (Read This If You Know Nothing About the Project)\n\n> [!note] This note assumes zero prior context. If you already know what CausalOps is, skip to [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]].\n\n## The Problem CausalOps Solves\n\nLarge language models are very good at producing *convincing* explanations. They are equally good at producing convincing explanations that are **completely unsupported by evidence**.\n\nMost \"AI agent\" systems let an LLM do all three of these steps itself:\n1. Generate a hypothesis (\"this incident was caused by X\")\n2. Generate the supporting evidence\n3. Explain why the evidence proves the hypothesis\n\nThe result reads well but has no actual statistical foundation — the LLM is grading its own homework.\n\n## The Core Design Principle\n\n> *\"The LLM proposes hypotheses. Deterministic code falsifies them.\"*\n\nThis is CausalOps's one-sentence design philosophy, and it shows up everywhere in the codebase as a hard rule. Concretely:\n\n- The LLM (an **agent swarm** — see below) is allowed to *design* a causal hypothesis: \"maybe patching this vulnerability reduces lateral movement.\"\n- The LLM is **never** allowed to invent the data that tests that hypothesis.\n- A separate, deterministic **evidence compiler** (`dataset_compiler.py`) ingests real SIEM logs, CVE records, and incident reports, and only *that* real data is used to test the hypothesis.\n- Statistical libraries (`DoWhy`, `statsmodels`) — not the LLM — compute whether the hypothesis holds up.\n- If the evidence is too weak (fewer than 50 complete observations, fewer than 10 treated/control rows, no observed variation), the system **refuses to produce a number**. It returns `method: \"withheld:data_quality_gates\"` instead of a fabricated Average Treatment Effect (ATE).\n\n*This refusal-when-uncertain behavior is treated as a **feature**, not a bug.* A system that always gives you an answer is less trustworthy than one that sometimes says \"the evidence doesn't support a conclusion yet.\"\n\n## What \"CausalOps\" Actually Does, End to End\n\nA user submits an incident description in plain English (e.g. \"suspected lateral movement via RDP in the finance segment\"). CausalOps then:\n\n1. **Decomposes** the incident into investigation tracks (an orchestrator agent).\n2. **Investigates** — parent and child agents write decision memos from different perspectives (containment, evidence-gathering, etc.).\n3. **Evaluates** the memos and ranks the proposed strategies.\n4. **Hypothesizes** a causal graph (a DAG — directed acyclic graph — of what causes what).\n5. **Compiles evidence** — the deterministic compiler turns raw evidence records into a clean statistical dataset, refusing anything an LLM generated itself.\n6. **Estimates** — DoWhy computes the causal effect, or withholds it if the data doesn't support one.\n7. **Validates the graph** — a separate causal-discovery pass (PC algorithm) checks the LLM's proposed DAG against the actual evidence and prunes edges that aren't statistically supported.\n8. **Reasons** — a deterministic reasoning layer looks for anomalies and drafts recommended actions.\n9. **Learns** — a reinforcement-learning loop updates policy priors based on how well past strategies performed.\n10. **Remembers** — the run becomes part of a persistent 5-dimensional knowledge graph *(this is a separate, pre-existing system from the memory layer this PR adds — see the callout below)*.\n\n> [!warning] Two different \"memory\" systems exist in this codebase — don't confuse them.\n> - The **5D Spatiotemporal Knowledge Graph** (`graph_5d.py`) already existed before this PR. It's a `(subject, predicate, object, time, location)` graph that powers reinforcement learning, historical replay, and visualization *within a single investigation's evidence*.\n> - The **Persistent Semantic Memory Layer** (this PR's subject) is new. It works *across* runs — it's what lets the system recognize \"this looks like the incident from three weeks ago,\" which the 5D graph alone cannot do.\n> See [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for full detail on the new system.\n\n## Why \"Agent Swarm,\" Not \"One Agent\"\n\nCausalOps deliberately uses a *hierarchy* of specialized agents rather than one large LLM call:\n\n- **Orchestrator** — decomposes the incident, decides how many \"parent\" investigation tracks to spin up\n- **Parent agents** — one per track, each spawning child agents\n- **Child agents** — narrow-focus specialists (e.g. \"Evidence & Causal Measurement Analyst\") that each write one decision memo\n- **Evaluator** — ranks the memos\n- **Causal Architect** — proposes the DAG\n- **Reasoner** — deterministic anomaly detection\n\nAgents can also **evolve** — a deterministic steady-state island evolutionary algorithm (not an LLM) tunes each agent's \"policy\" (traits like `evidence_weight`, `causal_focus`, `risk_aversion`) across runs, and reinforcement learning further refines these policies based on how well past investigations performed.\n\n## The Execution Path That Actually Runs in Production\n\nThere are two versions of the coordination logic in this codebase:\n\n- `src/graph.py` — a LangGraph state-graph implementation. **This is reference-only.** Its own docstring says it is deprecated for execution.\n- `src/coordinator/runner.py::execute_run()` — the **real** execution path, an async state machine that persists progress to SQLite between each phase.\n\nThis distinction matters for the memory layer work specifically: the new `memory_retrieve`/`memory_write` phases were added to `coordinator/runner.py`, not `graph.py`, because that's what actually runs.\n\n## The Technology Stack, Briefly\n\n| Layer | Technology |\n|---|---|\n| Chat LLM | NVIDIA Nemotron (primary) → Gemini (fallback) → Azure OpenAI (final fallback) |\n| Causal inference | DoWhy + statsmodels |\n| Causal discovery | PC algorithm (conditional independence testing) |\n| Event bus | Kafka (via Redpanda) |\n| Run persistence | SQLite (`data/runs.db`) |\n| **Memory layer (this PR)** | **Supabase (Postgres + pgvector) + Gemini embeddings + standalone MCP server** |\n| Frontend | React 19 + TanStack Start |\n| Backend | FastAPI |\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nNow that you know what CausalOps *is*, [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] explains exactly what this PR added to it.\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, memory-layer, architecture, implementation]\n---\n\n# The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component\n\n> [!info] This is the deep-dive technical note. If you need the short version first, read [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]].\n\nThe roadmap asked for five things. All five are implemented, tested, and verified live. This note explains each one — what it is, why it was built that way, and exactly how its correctness was proven (not assumed).\n\n## 1. Vector Retrieval\n\n**What it is:** every completed run's task description is turned into a numeric vector (\"embedding\") and stored in Postgres using the `pgvector` extension. When a new incident comes in, the system embeds *its* description and asks the database for the most similar past runs — mathematically, this means finding embeddings with the smallest angular distance (cosine similarity).\n\n**The file:** `src/memory/embedder.py` — one function, `embed_text(text: str) -> list[float]`.\n\n**A notable implementation decision — and why it changed mid-project:** the original plan used Azure OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small`. Azure's embedding credits were exhausted during development, so this was switched to **Gemini's `gemini-embedding-001`**, called through Gemini's OpenAI-compatible endpoint and truncated to 1536 dimensions (to match the database column, which was already sized for that dimensionality). This is *independent* of which LLM handles chat/reasoning — even after the codebase later switched its primary chat model to NVIDIA Nemotron (in unrelated work), the embedder kept using Gemini directly, because `embedder.py` never routes through the shared chat-LLM client (`src/llm.py`) at all — it makes its own direct API call. This decoupling turned out to matter a lot when this branch had to be reconciled with the NVIDIA-backend changes — see [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]].\n\n**Reliability:** 3-attempt exponential backoff (1s / 2s / 4s) on transient API failures.\n\n**How correctness was proven, not assumed:** every integration test in `tests/memory/` that touches embeddings runs against the *real* Gemini API and the *real* Supabase project — there is no mocking of the embedding call anywhere in the test suite that actually exercises retrieval.\n\n## 2. Knowledge Graph (Graph Traversal)\n\n**What it is:** entities — assets, MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, CVEs, and causal-graph node names — are extracted from every run's evidence and causal graph, and persisted as **nodes** and **edges** in three tables: `memory_entities` (the nodes) and `memory_entity_edges` (the relationships), tied back to `memory_runs` (which run created them).\n\n**The file:** `src/memory/extractor.py` — pure Python, **zero LLM calls**, entirely deterministic regex/dict extraction. This matters: entity extraction for the memory layer follows the exact same \"no LLM generates data rows\" principle that governs the rest of CausalOps (see [[01 - What is CausalOps (Project Primer)]]) — an LLM never gets to invent what counts as an \"asset\" or a \"technique.\"\n\n**Two extraction rules worth knowing precisely** (because they explain behavior that can otherwise look like a bug):\n- An asset↔technique edge is only created when *both* a valid `asset_id` **and** a technique ID matching the MITRE pattern (`T####` or `T####.###`) appear in the *same* evidence record. An asset mentioned without a technique produces no edge at all.\n- A causal-graph edge is only created between two nodes that were *both* already extracted as entities — this is a hard FK-safety rule (see `build_edges()`'s own docstring: \"entities not extracted... won't exist as rows... yet\").\n\n**Important scope note — \"graph traversal\" here means single-hop lookup, not multi-hop pathfinding.** The tool `get_entity_relationships()` (backed by the `get_entity_neighborhood` Postgres RPC) returns one entity's *direct* neighbors — it does not walk multiple hops to find indirect relationships. This matches what was actually scoped from the start; deeper traversal is listed as future work in [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]].\n\n**A real bug found and fixed during code review:** the original write path inserted new edges every time a run was written to memory, with no protection against duplicates. If `write_run()` was ever called twice for the same `run_id` (a retry, a rerun, a test), edges would double. **Fixed:** the write path now deletes any existing edges for that `run_id` before inserting the current set, making the write idempotent. This was verified live: two consecutive writes with identical input now produce exactly one edge, not two.\n\n## 3. Temporal Indexing\n\n**What it is:** similarity search doesn't just rank by textual similarity — it multiplies similarity by a **time-decay weight**, so a very similar incident from yesterday outranks an equally similar one from six months ago.\n\n**The formula:** `temporal_weight = exp(-0.023 × age_in_days)`. With λ = 0.023, this gives a **30-day half-life** — a run's weight roughly halves every 30 days.\n\n**Where it lives:** entirely inside a Postgres function, `search_similar_runs()` (see [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]]), not in Python. `weighted_score = similarity × temporal_weight` is what actually determines ranking.\n\n**How correctness was proven — this is one of the more interesting verification stories in this whole project:** the original implementation plan assumed testing decay math would require a raw-SQL test fixture, since the normal write path always lets Postgres default `created_at` to `now()`. That assumption turned out to be wrong. `created_at` is a completely ordinary column with no protecting trigger — a plain REST `.update()` call after the initial write backdates it just fine. This was discovered and verified *live*, before any test code was written: a row was written, backdated 30 days via a simple update call, and re-queried — its `weighted_score` came back at **`0.5016`**, which matches `exp(-0.023 × 30) = 0.50158...` to four decimal places. The formal test (`tests/memory/test_temporal_decay.py`) simply codifies this exact live-verified approach.\n\n## 4. MCP Server\n\n**What it is:** a standalone process exposing four tools over the **Model Context Protocol** (MCP) — the same protocol Claude Desktop and Claude Code use to give an AI agent tool access. This means Claude Code itself (or any other MCP-compatible agent) can directly query CausalOps's memory — which is exactly how several of this session's own verification steps worked, by literally calling these tools the same way a production agent would.\n\n**The four tools**, all in `src/memory/mcp_server.py`:\n| Tool | What it does |\n|---|---|\n| `search_similar_incidents` | vector + temporal-decay search over past runs |\n| `get_entity_relationships` | single-hop entity neighborhood lookup |\n| `get_asset_timeline` | chronological edges touching one asset over a trailing window |\n| `write_run_to_memory` | embeds, upserts, and indexes a completed run |\n\n**A critical architecture decision, stated explicitly so it doesn't get \"fixed\" by accident later:** this server is **never mounted inside the main FastAPI app** (`api.py`). It runs as its own process (`python -m memory.mcp_server`), reachable either over **stdio** (how Claude Desktop/Code spawn it directly) or **SSE** on port 8001 (how the Docker Compose deployment exposes it). This was a deliberate architecture-decision-record choice logged early in the project, and one of the real bugs fixed in this PR was exactly a violation of this boundary — see below.\n\n**A real deployment bug found and fixed:** the server's `__main__` block only ever read `MCP_TRANSPORT` from the environment and never passed `host`/`port` through to `mcp.run()` for the SSE case. This meant the Docker Compose service's `MCP_PORT=8001` setting was silently ignored, and the server always bound to FastMCP's own default (`127.0.0.1:8000`) — making the container **completely unreachable** from the Docker host, despite `docker-compose.yml` mapping port 8001. Fixed, and verified live with the actual running container: `curl http://localhost:8001/sse` returned `200 OK` with `content-type: text/event-stream`.\n\n**A second, more subtle deployment bug found later (via automated code review), in a *setup script*, not the server itself:** `setup-claude-code.sh` — a helper script that scaffolds a `.claude/` folder for new contributors — generated a `.mcp.json` pointing at `http://localhost:8000/mcp`, an HTTP bridge that was never built (a leftover from an earlier design that predated the \"standalone server\" decision above). Fixed to spawn the server directly over stdio instead, matching how it actually runs. Investigating this also surfaced that the *whole file* still described the pre-pivot design (Azure embeddings instead of Gemini, wrong package version pins, a scope line claiming the server *should* be mounted in `api.py`) — all corrected in the same pass.\n\n**How correctness was proven — this is the standout testing achievement of this whole PR.** Before this PR, the *only* test of the MCP layer called the tool functions directly with a mocked store (`mcp_server.search_similar_incidents(...)`) — proving the Python function delegates correctly, but proving nothing about the MCP *protocol* itself. This PR adds `tests/memory/test_mcp_bridge.py`, which opens a real `fastmcp.Client` session against the live server object and drives an actual write→search round trip **through the real MCP protocol** (tool discovery, argument validation, response serialization) against the live Supabase project — this is genuinely different from, and strictly stronger than, calling a Python function directly. Full detail on why this distinction matters: [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]].\n\n## 5. Agent Integration\n\n**What it is:** two new phases in the coordinator's execution pipeline (`src/coordinator/runner.py`):\n- **`memory_retrieve`** — runs before the orchestrator decomposes the incident. Retrieves the 3 most similar past runs and injects a summary into the orchestrator's prompt (via `_format_memory_context()` in `agents.py`), so the LLM's decomposition is informed by what happened last time.\n- **`memory_write`** — runs after *every* run completes (see the important nuance below), persisting the finished run's task description, embedding, entities, and edges.\n\n**The single most important design guarantee in this whole feature:** both phases are **non-fatal by design**. If Supabase is down, or the embedding API times out, the exception is logged and swallowed — a memory-layer outage can *never* fail an actual investigation. This is enforced at two levels: inside `memory/nodes.py`'s own functions, and again by the coordinator's wrapper functions around them.\n\n**A subtlety worth understanding precisely — this only became relevant because of the branch-reconciliation work (see [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]]):** the coordinator gained a new `execution_mode` concept (\"standard\" vs. \"deep\") from unrelated work landing on `main` while this branch was in flight. The decision made here was to keep `memory_retrieve` and `memory_write` running **unconditionally, regardless of mode** — a \"standard\" (fast) run deserves to be remembered too, not just a \"deep\" one. This was a deliberate design call, not an accident of the merge.\n\n**A real bug in `_memory_configured()`, found by automated code review:** the function that decides \"is the memory layer even configured?\" originally treated *any* non-empty `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` value as configured — including `.env.example`'s own literal placeholder text, `\"your-service-role-key-here\"`. This meant a fresh clone that hadn't yet filled in real credentials would still *try* to make real network calls on every single run, fail, and log noisy exceptions. Fixed to use the same placeholder-detection heuristic (`\"your-\" not in key`) the test suite's own credential check already used.\n\n## Cross-Reference: The Roadmap Sentence, Clause by Clause\n\n| Roadmap clause | Satisfied by |\n|---|---|\n| \"vector retrieval\" | Component 1 above |\n| \"graph traversal\" | Component 2 above (single-hop, by design) |\n| \"temporal indexing\" | Component 3 above |\n| \"persistent contextual awareness across tasks\" | Component 5 above |\n| \"longitudinal reasoning, adaptive learning, higher-order strategic coordination\" | *Not a separately-built mechanism* — this is the intended **emergent effect** of the orchestrator now having access to real historical context. It is not something a unit test can assert; it's a description of expected downstream benefit, not a checklist item. Be precise about this distinction if asked in the meeting: the *infrastructure* is built and tested; whether it measurably improves reasoning over time is an open, unmeasured question. |\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nFor the database side of all this (exact schema, migrations, RLS decisions): [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]].\nFor the MCP protocol testing story in full: [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]].\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, memory-layer, supabase, database, sql]\n---\n\n# Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer\n\n> [!info] This note explains the database side of the memory layer in detail: what tables exist, why Row-Level Security is configured the way it is, what got hardened and why, and how the schema is now kept in version control.\n\n## Why Supabase\n\nSupabase is Postgres with extensions and a hosted REST/RPC layer on top. The two features that specifically make it the right fit here:\n- **`pgvector`** — a native Postgres extension for storing and searching high-dimensional embedding vectors efficiently (via HNSW indexing).\n- **PostgREST** — every table and function is automatically exposed as a callable REST/RPC endpoint, which is how the Python backend (`src/memory/store.py`) and the MCP server both talk to it without hand-writing HTTP routes.\n\n**Project ID:** `glbmdbwqmuttykhicasq`\n\n## The Schema, Table by Table\n\n### `memory_runs`\nOne row per completed CausalOps run.\n\n| Column | Type | Purpose |\n|---|---|---|\n| `run_id` | `text unique` | ties back to the coordinator's run |\n| `task_description` | `text` | the original incident description |\n| `task_embedding` | `vector(1536)` | the Gemini embedding, indexed via HNSW |\n| `memos`, `causal_graph`, `estimate_report` | `jsonb` | the run's actual output artifact |\n| `created_at` | `timestamptz` | drives temporal decay — see [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] |\n\n### `memory_entities`\nOne row per unique `(entity_type, entity_value)` pair ever seen — assets, MITRE techniques, CVEs, or causal-graph node names. This table is **deduplicated across all runs** via a unique constraint on `(entity_type, entity_value)` — the same asset seen in ten different incidents is still one row, with `last_seen` updated each time.\n\n### `memory_entity_edges`\nOne row per relationship between two entities, tagged with which run (`source_run_id`) produced it. Foreign keys to both `memory_entities` (on both `source_entity_id` and `target_entity_id`) and to `memory_runs.run_id`, all with `ON DELETE CASCADE`.\n\n### The two RPC (remote procedure call) functions\n- **`search_similar_runs(query_embedding, match_count, decay_lambda)`** — the vector-similarity + temporal-decay search described in [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]]. Runs entirely in SQL for performance — no round trip of raw vectors back to Python for scoring.\n- **`get_entity_neighborhood(p_entity_value, p_entity_type)`** — single-hop entity relationship lookup.\n\n## The Four Migrations (Now Tracked as Code)\n\nA real gap this PR closed: **the schema had never been captured as local migration files** — it existed only as SQL that had been run directly against the live project via tooling, with no record of it anywhere in the repository. If the project ever needed to be reproduced on a fresh Supabase instance, or if a disaster-recovery scenario arose, there was nothing to run. This is now fixed: `supabase/migrations/` contains the exact SQL that's actually live on the project, pulled directly from Supabase's own migration history table (not reconstructed from memory or guesswork):\n\n1. `enable_pgvector` — `CREATE EXTENSION vector`\n2. `create_memory_layer_schema` — the three tables, the HNSW index, and both RPC functions\n3. `enable_rls_memory_tables` — enables Row-Level Security (see below)\n4. `harden_memory_functions_and_index_fk` — *(new in this PR)* — see \"What Got Hardened,\" below\n\n## Row-Level Security: Enabled, Zero Policies — This Is Correct, Not a Bug\n\nIf you look at the tables in the Supabase dashboard, you'll see RLS is **enabled** on all three memory tables, but **no policies exist**. At first glance this looks incomplete. It is not.\n\n**Postgres semantics: RLS enabled + zero policies = deny-all for every role except the table owner and any role with the `BYPASSRLS` attribute.** The Python backend authenticates using `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, which *does* carry `BYPASSRLS` in Supabase — so backend writes work, while the anon/publishable key (used only by the frontend for unrelated auth flows) is correctly locked out of these tables entirely. This was reviewed and confirmed deliberately as part of this PR: nothing in the frontend queries these tables directly, so deny-all-except-service-role is exactly the right posture. **Do not \"fix\" this by adding permissive RLS policies** unless the memory layer is ever exposed to non-backend callers.\n\n## What Got Hardened (New Migration, This PR)\n\nSupabase's own advisory linter — run as a matter of routine after any schema change, not because anything was suspected to be wrong — surfaced two real, previously-unaddressed issues:\n\n1. **`function_search_path_mutable` (WARN, security)** on *both* RPC functions. Postgres functions without a pinned `search_path` are vulnerable to search-path-hijacking in certain privilege-escalation scenarios. **Fixed:** both functions now have `SET search_path = public, extensions` pinned explicitly.\n2. **`unindexed_foreign_keys` (INFO, performance)** — `memory_entity_edges.target_entity_id` had a foreign key with no covering index, meaning the entity-neighborhood join was doing more work than necessary. **Fixed:** added `memory_entity_edges_target_idx`.\n\nBoth fixes were applied live to the project and reverified afterward: the advisories are gone, and the full test suite (22 memory tests) still passes with zero behavior change — this was a pure hardening pass, not a feature change.\n\n## Retention: A Manual Query, Deliberately Not Automated\n\nThere is currently **no automatic deletion** of old `memory_runs` or `memory_entities` rows. This was a deliberate choice, not an oversight — see [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]] for the reasoning. What exists instead is a documented, copy-pasteable manual query (in the project's `CLAUDE.md`):\n\n```sql\ndelete from memory_runs where created_at < now() - interval '90 days';\n```\n\n`memory_entity_edges` rows cascade-delete automatically when their parent run is deleted. Orphaned entities (no edges left pointing at them) are left in place deliberately — they're a shared, cross-run knowledge graph, not scoped to any single run's lifetime, so an entity remaining in the table after its originating run is pruned is not \"stale data,\" it's the graph doing its job.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nFor how the MCP server actually talks to this schema over the network: [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]].\nFor the full list of what's still open around this data layer: [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]].\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, memory-layer, mcp, testing, protocol]\n---\n\n# The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge\n\n> [!info] This note goes deep on one specific, easy-to-underestimate distinction: the difference between *testing that a function works* and *testing that the protocol wrapping it works*. Getting this distinction right was one of the more valuable pieces of engineering judgment in this whole project.\n\n## What MCP Is, in One Paragraph\n\nThe **Model Context Protocol** (MCP) is the mechanism by which an AI agent — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or any other MCP-compatible client — discovers and calls tools exposed by an external server. It's not a REST API in the conventional sense: it has its own handshake, its own tool-discovery step (the client asks \"what tools do you have?\" before calling any of them), its own JSON-schema-based argument validation, and its own structured-content response format. A server can expose tools correctly *as Python functions* while the MCP wrapping around them is subtly broken — wrong transport, wrong port, a tool registered with the wrong name — and a test that only calls the Python function directly would never catch that.\n\n## Why This Distinction Mattered Here, Concretely\n\nBefore this PR, `tests/memory/test_mcp_tools.py` looked like a reasonable MCP test. It mocked `SupabaseMemoryStore` and called `mcp_server.search_similar_incidents(\"...\", k=2)` directly. This *is* a valid, useful unit test — it proves the tool wrapper correctly delegates to the store. But it is not a test of the MCP server *as an MCP server*. It never opens a client session, never goes through tool discovery, never exercises argument validation against the tool's declared schema.\n\nMeanwhile, the actual deployed server had a **real, live bug** in exactly the part this kind of test can't see: its `__main__` block silently ignored `MCP_HOST`/`MCP_PORT` for the SSE transport, meaning the Docker-deployed server was completely unreachable despite the container appearing to run fine (see [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]] and [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for the fix). **That specific class of bug is exactly the kind a protocol-level test would have caught, and a function-level test cannot.**\n\n## The Fix: Two New, Genuinely Different Kinds of Test\n\n### 1. In-memory protocol tests (fast, no credentials) — added to `test_mcp_tools.py`\n\n```python\nasync def _list() -> list[str]:\n    async with Client(mcp_server.mcp) as client:\n        tools = await client.list_tools()\n        return [tool.name for tool in tools]\n```\n\nPassing the live `FastMCP` object *directly* to `fastmcp.Client` (rather than a URL) makes the client infer an **in-memory transport** — no Docker, no network socket, but the *same protocol layer* as the real deployment: real tool discovery, real JSON-schema argument validation, real response serialization. This is the key insight that makes rigorous MCP testing cheap: you don't need a running server process to test the protocol correctly, you just need the server *object*.\n\n### 2. A live, real-infrastructure protocol round trip — a brand-new file, `test_mcp_bridge.py`\n\nThis test does something no prior test in the codebase did: it opens a real `Client` session and calls `write_run_to_memory` followed by `search_similar_incidents`, **through the actual MCP protocol**, against the **real, live Supabase project** — with the same tagged-UUID-and-cleanup discipline used elsewhere in the test suite, so repeated runs never pollute production data. This is a strictly stronger guarantee than either \"the function works\" (the old test) or \"the protocol works against a mock\" (test 1 above) — it proves the whole chain, end to end, for real.\n\n**This exact pattern was proven by hand before a single line of test code was written** — a live smoke script was run first (write → search → assert the written run appears in search results → clean up), confirmed working, and *then* turned into the formal test. This \"prove it live first, write the test second\" discipline shows up repeatedly in this project — see [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]] for why that ordering matters.\n\n## The Live Deployment Verification (Docker/SSE)\n\nSeparately from the in-process protocol tests above, the actual Docker-deployed server was verified live, end to end, in its real deployed form:\n\n```\n$ docker ps --filter name=mcp\ncausalops-mcp-1   Up 3 hours   0.0.0.0:8001->8001/tcp\n\n$ curl -sv --max-time 3 http://localhost:8001/sse\n< HTTP/1.1 200 OK\n< content-type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8\n```\n\nThis confirms the fix to the `MCP_HOST`/`MCP_PORT` bug actually works in the environment it will actually run in (Docker Compose), not just in a unit test's simulated environment.\n\n## The Automated Code Review Round (GitHub Copilot) — What It Caught Here Specifically\n\nAn automated PR review pass caught two real, previously-unnoticed problems, both in `setup-claude-code.sh` (a contributor-onboarding script, not the server itself):\n\n1. The generated `.mcp.json` pointed at `http://localhost:8000/mcp` — an HTTP bridge into the main FastAPI app that was never built, and never should be (see the \"never mounted in api.py\" rule in [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]]).\n2. A generated test-instructions file (`commands/test-memory.md`) told a new contributor to `curl` that same non-existent endpoint.\n\nBoth were fixed by pointing the generated config at the real stdio-spawned server instead. Investigating *why* these were wrong surfaced that the entire onboarding script predated the \"standalone MCP server\" architecture decision — it still described mounting the server inside `api.py`, still referenced Azure embeddings instead of Gemini, and still checked for package versions (`fastmcp==3.2.4`) that are actually uninstallable alongside the pinned Supabase client version. All of this was corrected in the same pass, not just the two specific lines flagged.\n\n## The Takeaway, for a Meeting or an Interview\n\nIf asked \"how do you know the MCP integration actually works, not just that the code compiles\" — this is the answer: there are now three independent layers of proof (mocked-store protocol test, live in-memory protocol round trip, and live Docker/SSE deployment check), each catching a different class of failure the others structurally cannot.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nFor the reconciliation work that happened around this same code during the branch rebase: [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]].\nFor the full testing philosophy this project follows: [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]].\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, git, rebase, merge-conflicts, engineering-process]\n---\n\n# Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story\n\n> [!info] If someone in the meeting asks \"why did this PR touch 111 files when the feature is really just a memory layer\" — this note is the answer. This was, honestly, the hardest and highest-risk part of the entire body of work, harder than writing the memory layer itself.\n\n## The Situation\n\nThis feature branch (`plan/persistent-memory-mcp`) was created and developed against a specific point in the project's history. By the time it was ready to open as a pull request, the target branch (`main`) had moved forward **five separate commits** with substantial, unrelated work:\n\n1. A **new primary LLM backend** — NVIDIA's Nemotron model, via NIM/API Catalog, with Gemini demoted to a fallback (used only when `NVIDIA_API_KEY` is unset) and Azure OpenAI further demoted to a final fallback.\n2. A new **`execution_mode`** concept (\"standard\" vs. \"deep\") — a fast/cheap execution path (`_seed_standard_swarm`, local memo ranking, a deterministic causal fallback) alongside the original full multi-agent pipeline.\n3. A **\"5D-first\" result workspace** redesign on the frontend.\n4. New **visual regression test coverage**.\n5. A substantial **README rewrite**.\n\nOpening a pull request without reconciling these first would have produced a PR full of misleading, conflict-laden diff noise, and — more importantly — genuine risk of the memory-layer code silently breaking against the *current*, not the *historical*, state of the coordinator. **The decision made here was to stop and reconcile properly before opening anything**, rather than let a reviewer discover the conflicts.\n\n## The Reconciliation Method\n\nA `git merge --squash` was used to bring the entire feature branch's changes onto current `main` as one set of conflicts to resolve **once**, rather than replaying five original commits individually through a `git rebase` (which risks resolving overlapping conflicts multiple times across different commits in the replay sequence — more error-prone, not less, for a divergence this size). This did mean the five original commits collapsed into one on the pushed branch — a deliberate, disclosed tradeoff, not an accident (the original granular history was kept on a local backup branch rather than discarded).\n\n## What Actually Had Conflicts, and How Each Was Resolved\n\nNine files had genuine, hand-resolved conflicts (not mechanical auto-merges):\n\n| File | The conflict | The resolution |\n|---|---|---|\n| `src/coordinator/runner.py` | The new `execution_mode` branching had to be interleaved with the new `memory_retrieve`/`memory_write` phases | Memory phases now bracket the *entire* pipeline unconditionally, regardless of mode — see [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] |\n| `app/src/routes/run.ts` | One side deleted the file (an intentionally-removed frontend mock), the other side had cosmetically modified it | Took the deletion — the file's removal was deliberate upstream work, and this branch's change to it was purely cosmetic |\n| `app/src/components/.../GraphWorkspace.tsx` | A new file added upstream, under the *old* pre-rebrand directory path | Relocated to the renamed directory, its internal import fixed to match |\n| `.env.example`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.gitignore` | Both sides had added genuinely different, non-overlapping content | Hand-merged — neither side's additions were dropped |\n| `README.md` | The most complex conflict: an old \"Future Enhancements\" roadmap list (containing the *exact sentence this whole PR implements* — see [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]]) had landed under the wrong heading purely because of how the diff lined up | Relocated to a new, dedicated \"Persistent Semantic Memory Layer\" section; the Future Work → Knowledge Graph roadmap items this PR actually delivers were marked done rather than left listed as still-planned |\n| Every file referencing a `HIVEMIND_*`-prefixed environment variable | `main` had added *three new* environment variables in this old naming scheme, after this branch had already renamed everything else to `CAUSALOPS_*` | Renamed for consistency, across every consuming file and the two tests that set them |\n\n## A Real Bug This Reconciliation Introduced, and How It Was Caught\n\nThis is the single most instructive part of the whole story. After all conflicts were resolved and the full test suite passed, a **second, unrelated task** (responding to automated code-review feedback) required re-running the memory test suite live. That rerun failed — and the failure was not in any code touched by that second task. It was a **latent bug the rebase itself had silently introduced**, sitting undetected through the initial \"all tests pass\" check.\n\n**What happened:** `tests/memory/test_end_to_end.py` calls `execute_run()` without specifying an `execution_mode` — which didn't exist as a concept when this test was originally written. Because `execution_mode` now defaults to `\"standard\"`, the coordinator started routing through the **new** fast-path functions (`_seed_standard_swarm`, `_run_fast_causal_loop`) instead of the original full pipeline this test's fakes were built for. Those new functions call things (`publish_artifact()`, and imports from a `causal` module the test's fake replacement doesn't define) that the test's mocks never anticipated, because they didn't exist yet when the test was written.\n\n**Why the first test run didn't catch this:** the first \"all tests pass\" check happened immediately after conflict resolution, in the same verification pass — and simply calling the same test twice with the same code produces the same *deterministic* result every time. This wasn't a flaky test; it was a real, reproducible failure that had been sitting there since the rebase, only surfaced because someone happened to run that specific test file again for an unrelated reason.\n\n**The fix:** pin `execution_mode=\"deep\"` explicitly on both `execute_run()` calls in that test, restoring the exact pipeline shape its fakes were always built for — matching the convention the codebase's *other* coordinator test (`test_coordinator_runner.py`) already used (it explicitly parameterizes `execution_mode` rather than relying on the default, precisely to avoid this class of problem).\n\n**The lesson worth stating explicitly, because it's genuinely useful career-relevant judgment, not just a war story:** *\"all tests passed right after I made the change\" is not the same claim as \"this change has no latent bugs.\"* A test suite only proves what it actually exercises. Rerunning tests later, for an unrelated reason, is what caught this — which is itself an argument for re-verifying rather than treating a single green run as permanent proof.\n\n## Silent Breakage That Had Nothing to Do With Merge Conflicts At All\n\nOne more real bug was found during this reconciliation, in a file that had **zero conflict markers** — meaning Git's automatic merge considered it perfectly clean. `app/src/components/causalops/ScenarioBuilder.tsx` had a new import line, added by `main`'s changes, referencing `@/lib/hivemind-types` — a module path that had already been renamed to `@/lib/causalops-types` by this branch, in a part of the file the automatic merge never flagged as conflicting because only one side had touched that specific line. This is a structurally important point: **\"no conflict markers\" is not the same claim as \"nothing broke.\"** It was caught by a deliberate, repo-wide grep for leftover old-naming references *after* resolving the visible conflicts — not by the merge tool, and not by any test.\n\n## What This Demonstrates as an Engineering Skill\n\nIf this comes up in an interview: this is a concrete example of **safely reconciling a long-lived feature branch with a fast-moving main branch** — a routine, high-stakes task in any real engineering team, and one where the actual risk isn't \"will Git show a conflict marker,\" it's \"will something silently behave differently after the merge succeeds.\" The two real bugs found here (the silent broken import, and the latent test failure from a changed default) are both examples of exactly that risk, caught by disciplined re-verification rather than by trusting a clean merge or a single passing test run.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nFor how every claim in this story was actually verified (not just asserted): [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]].\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/06 - Testing & Verification Methodology.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, testing, verification, engineering-process]\n---\n\n# Testing & Verification Methodology\n\n> [!info] This note is about *how* \"done\" was actually established throughout this project — a repeated discipline of proving things live before trusting them, cross-checking claims against reality instead of assuming, and treating an automated review pass as a genuine second opinion rather than a formality.\n\n## The Core Discipline: Prove It Live, *Then* Write the Test\n\nA pattern repeats throughout this whole project: before writing a formal automated test for a new piece of behavior, a small, throwaway script was run **against the real infrastructure** (the actual Supabase project, the actual Gemini API, the actual MCP server) to confirm the behavior works *at all*, before committing to a specific test design. Only after that live confirmation was the formal `pytest` test written, matching the already-proven shape.\n\nConcrete examples of this from the project:\n- The temporal-decay math (see [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]]) — backdating a row and checking its weighted score was done live, by hand, *before* `test_temporal_decay.py` existed. The live result (`0.5016`, matching the formula to four decimal places) is what gave confidence the test design was even worth writing.\n- The MCP protocol round trip (see [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]]) — a live write→search→cleanup script was run against the real server object and the real Supabase project before `test_mcp_bridge.py` was written.\n- The idempotent-edge-write fix and the DB-side asset-timeline query refactor (both prompted by automated code review, below) were each verified with a standalone live script *in addition to* the existing test suite — because the existing tests used loose assertions (`isinstance(result, list)`) that wouldn't have caught a regression in either fix.\n\n**Why this order matters, as a general practice:** a test written against an *assumed* behavior can pass while testing the wrong thing entirely. Proving the behavior live first means the test is validated against reality, not against an assumption about reality.\n\n## Independent Cross-Checking, Not Just Trusting a Clean Run\n\nSeveral points in this project involved a specific kind of verification: comparing a result against an independent baseline, rather than trusting a single measurement in isolation.\n\n- **Before assuming a lint/type-check finding was newly introduced, it was checked against the actual unmodified target branch.** A git worktree was used to check out the real `upstream/main` in isolation and run the exact same `pyright`/`eslint` commands there — confirming, for instance, that pyright's 56 errors and eslint's 159 findings were byte-for-byte identical whether or not this branch's changes were present. This converts \"I think this is pre-existing\" from a guess into a verified fact.\n- **Before trusting a CI failure was \"the same issue seen locally,\"** the CI workflow file itself was read to reproduce the *exact* command CI runs (`python -m ruff check .` from the repo root, using a specific pinned dependency set from `requirements-dev.txt`) — which turned out to matter, because CI's pinned ruff version doesn't flag the same rule set as the local development environment's ruff version. Two backend lint findings looked different between CI and local until this was accounted for.\n\n## Treating Automated Code Review as a Real Second Opinion\n\nWhen GitHub Copilot's automated review returned five inline findings on the pull request, **every single one was independently re-verified against the actual code before being acted on** — not applied on faith, and not dismissed on faith either. All five turned out to be real:\n\n1. A stale `.mcp.json` generation pointing at a non-existent endpoint\n2. A stale test-instructions file curling the same non-existent endpoint\n3. A credential-placeholder-detection gap in `_memory_configured()`\n4. A non-idempotent entity-edge write\n5. An inefficient (full-scan-then-filter) database query\n\nEach fix was then *itself* verified live — not just re-run through the existing test suite, since two of the five (the idempotency fix and the query refactor) involved behavior the existing tests were too loosely written to actually catch a regression in. New, targeted live smoke tests were written and run specifically to confirm each fix worked as intended, in addition to the formal test suite passing.\n\n**A sixth bug was found during this same pass — one Copilot's review never flagged at all** (the `execution_mode` default causing a latent test failure, fully explained in [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]]). This is worth naming explicitly: automated review is a genuinely useful second opinion, but it is not exhaustive, and finding something it missed while independently verifying its own findings is exactly the kind of thing that should be expected from careful engineering, not treated as a fluke.\n\n## The Numbers, All Independently Reproduced More Than Once\n\n| Check | Result | Reproduced |\n|---|---|---|\n| `pytest tests/memory/ -v` (live Supabase + Gemini) | 22 passed, 0 skipped | Multiple times across the project, including after every fix |\n| `pytest tests/ -m \"not integration and not kafka\"` | 97 passed | Multiple times, confirming zero regressions from every change |\n| `ruff check .` (matching CI exactly) | Clean after fixes; 3 pre-existing findings confirmed not CI-blocking | Verified against a real worktree of `main` |\n| `npm run lint` (frontend) | Clean after fixes; 159 pre-existing findings confirmed identical to `main` | Verified against both `main` and the pre-rebase branch |\n| `npm run build` | Clean client + SSR build | Re-run after every frontend-touching change |\n\n## Why \"A Skip Is Not a Pass\" Was a Recurring Warning\n\nIntegration tests in this codebase are gated behind real credentials (`SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`) and skip automatically if those credentials aren't present in the process environment. This creates a specific trap: if credentials are configured in a `.env` file but that file isn't actually sourced into the shell before running `pytest`, every integration test silently **skips** rather than failing — and a skip can be misread, at a glance, as a clean pass. This project's own conventions guard against this explicitly: every integration test run in this work was preceded by `set -a && source .env && set +a` in the *same* shell invocation, and the resulting summary line was checked specifically for a skip count of zero, not just an absence of failures.\n\n## The Takeaway for a Meeting or an Interview\n\nIf asked \"how do you know this actually works, beyond 'the tests pass'\" — the honest, complete answer has three parts: (1) the behavior was proven live against real infrastructure before the test was even written, (2) claims about \"this is pre-existing, not something I broke\" were checked against an independent baseline rather than assumed, and (3) an automated second opinion was treated as genuinely useful — verified rather than blindly trusted, and it caught real things, and one more real thing was found that it missed.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nFor what's still explicitly open, and how to talk about this project going forward: [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]].\n"}`

That distinction (deliberate scoping decision vs. oversight) is itself worth being able to explain clearly — it's the difference between \"we ran out of time\" and \"we made a judgment call about what belongs in this change.\"\n\n## What's Actually Left — In Priority Order\n\n### 1. Automated memory-row retention (highest-value next step)\n**What exists today:** a manual, documented SQL query (see [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]]) — no scheduled job deletes anything automatically.\n**Why it was deliberately deferred, not built:** automating deletion is a bigger, harder-to-reverse commitment than it sounds — it means picking a specific retention window *before* there's real usage data to justify one, and it means running an unattended job that deletes production data on a schedule. The considered judgment was: build the manual escape hatch now, defer the automation decision until real usage patterns exist to inform it.\n**What it would take:** either a Supabase-native scheduled Edge Function, or enabling the `pg_cron` Postgres extension (currently *not* installed on the project, confirmed directly) and a scheduled SQL job calling the existing manual query.\n\n### 2. Multi-hop graph traversal and graph embeddings\n**What exists today:** single-hop entity-neighborhood lookup (`get_entity_relationships`) — see [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for exactly why this boundary exists.\n**What's still open:** the README's own \"Future Work\" section (updated as part of this PR to reflect what's actually done) lists \"graph embeddings\" (embedding the causal-graph *structure* itself, not just task descriptions) and \"multi-hop causal querying\" as the next steps in this specific area.\n\n### 3. A second, deeper automated code-review pass\nA follow-up review was explicitly requested — of every file touched by the branch-reconciliation work specifically (see [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]]), not just the new memory-layer code — since that reconciliation was hand-done and is exactly the kind of work most likely to hide something an initial pass missed. As of this writing, that second pass had not yet returned results.\n\n### 4. Temporal-decay math has an automated test now — but retention math doesn't have a corresponding automated audit\nThe decay *search* math is now proven correct (see [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]]). If automated retention (item 1) is ever built, its own correctness (e.g. \"does it actually only delete rows older than N days, and nothing else\") should get the same live-verification treatment described in [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]] before being trusted.\n\n## What NOT to Do Next (Explicitly, So It Doesn't Get \"Fixed\" By Accident)\n\n- **Do not add RLS policies** to the memory tables. Deny-all-except-service-role is a deliberate, reviewed decision (see [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]]), not an incomplete setup.\n- **Do not mount the MCP server inside `api.py`.** This has already been the subject of one real bug (a stale onboarding script assuming exactly this) — see [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]].\n- **Do not assume a clean CI run or a clean merge means nothing is broken** without the kind of independent re-verification described in [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]] — this project found two genuinely separate real bugs specifically *because* it didn't stop checking after the first green result.\n\n## How This Work Is Useful on a Resume, LinkedIn, or GitHub — For an Upcoming AI Engineer\n\nThis is worth being specific and honest about, rather than vague. The *feature itself* (\"I added a vector database to an AI agent\") is a fine one-liner, but it is not the most valuable or most differentiating thing to highlight. The process this project demonstrates is more valuable, and more rare, and is what should actually anchor how this gets described externally.\n\n### What to actually emphasize\n\n1. **Reconciling a long-lived feature branch with a fast-moving main branch, safely.** This is a routine, high-stakes task at any real engineering job, and most engineers have a story about getting it wrong. This project has a concrete, specific story about doing it carefully — including catching two real bugs the merge itself introduced, one of them completely invisible to Git's own conflict detection. **This is genuinely senior-level judgment**, not a beginner task, and it's rare to see it demonstrated this concretely in a portfolio piece.\n2. **Building retrieval-augmented memory for an agentic system** (vector search + knowledge graph + temporal decay) is a directly relevant, currently in-demand skill set — this maps precisely onto what production RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) and agent-memory systems look like in industry, described in the vocabulary the industry actually uses (embeddings, pgvector, temporal decay, MCP).\n3. **Treating an AI code-review tool as a genuine second opinion rather than a checkbox** — verifying every one of its findings, and finding one more real bug it missed — is a specific, demonstrable example of working *with* AI tooling critically rather than either blindly trusting it or ignoring it. This is an increasingly relevant skill to be able to speak to directly, given how much of the industry now uses these tools.\n4. **The MCP (Model Context Protocol) work specifically** is current, in-demand, and not yet common experience — MCP is the emerging standard for how AI agents connect to tools and data, and building a real MCP server (not a toy example) with genuine protocol-level test coverage is a concrete, specific, and current thing to be able to talk about.\n\n### A concrete way to phrase this for a resume or LinkedIn post (adapt freely, don't copy verbatim)\n\n> *Designed and shipped a persistent memory layer for a multi-agent causal-reasoning system: vector retrieval (pgvector), a cross-run entity knowledge graph, and temporal decay-weighted ranking, exposed via a standalone MCP server with full protocol-level test coverage. Reconciled the feature branch with five commits of unrelated upstream changes (new LLM backend, new execution-mode architecture), catching and fixing two real bugs introduced by the merge — including one invisible to Git's own conflict detection. Verified every AI-code-review finding independently before acting on it, and found an additional bug the review missed.*\n\n### For a GitHub portfolio / pinned repo description\n\nIf this repo (or a similar one) is used as a portfolio piece, the pull request itself (`darshgarg7/CausalOps#25`) is a legitimate, presentable artifact — not something to hide the mechanics of. A detailed, honest PR description and commit history (which this project has, deliberately) *is* the portfolio piece. A reviewer or interviewer who reads the actual commit messages and PR description gets a genuine, verifiable demonstration of engineering judgment, not just a claim about it.\n\n### What to be honest about, if asked directly\n\n- The \"longitudinal reasoning, adaptive learning, higher-order strategic coordination\" language from the original roadmap sentence is **aspirational** — the infrastructure enabling it is built and tested, but whether it produces measurably better reasoning over time has not been measured. Being precise about this distinction, rather than overclaiming it, is itself a signal of engineering maturity worth demonstrating.\n- Retention automation, multi-hop traversal, and a second review pass are genuinely unfinished — say so plainly rather than implying total completeness. A reviewer who asks \"what's left\" and gets a clear, prioritized answer (as in this note) reads as more credible than one who claims everything is done.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nIf you need the whole story again from the top: [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]].\n"}`

Every other note in this folder goes deeper on one specific piece of this work — links are at the bottom of every section.\n\n## The One-Sentence Version\n\nCausalOps agents used to start every incident investigation from zero — no memory of past runs, no cross-run entity tracking, no sense of \"have we seen something like this before.\" This PR gives them **persistent memory**: every completed run is embedded, indexed, and made retrievable, so the next similar incident automatically surfaces what happened last time, weighted by how recently it happened, and cross-referenced against a growing knowledge graph of assets, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and CVEs seen across every past investigation.\n\n## Why This Matters — The Business Case, Not Just the Technical One\n\nWithout this feature, every incident is investigated in isolation. With this feature, that prior investigation surfaces automatically, with its causal graph, its statistical estimate, and its outcome, *before* the orchestrator even starts decomposing the new incident. Full story: [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]].\n\n## What's Genuinely Left (Not Done, By Deliberate Choice — Not an Oversight)\n\nThree things were explicitly scoped *out* of this PR, each for a stated reason:\n\n1. **Automated memory-row retention/deletion** — a manual SQL query is documented instead; automating deletion is deferred until real usage data shows what retention window actually makes sense. Building an unattended job that deletes production data on a schedule, before there's evidence to size that schedule correctly, was judged premature.\n2. **Multi-hop graph traversal / graph embeddings** — the current graph traversal is single-hop entity-neighborhood lookup, which matches what was actually scoped from the start. Deeper traversal is genuine future work, not a corner that was cut.\n3. **A second, deeper Copilot re-review** of the merge-conflict-resolved files specifically — requested in the PR but not yet returned as of this writing.\n\nFull detail, prioritized, plus what to say if asked \"what's next\": [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]].\n\n## A Glossary, In Case the Meeting Includes Non-Technical Stakeholders\n\n- **Embedding** — a numeric representation of text (a list of ~1500 numbers) such that texts with similar *meaning* end up numerically close together. This is what makes \"find me past incidents similar to this one\" a mathematical operation rather than a keyword search.\n- **Vector database (pgvector)** — a database extension that can efficiently search millions of these numeric representations for the closest matches.\n- **Knowledge graph** — a network of entities (assets, techniques, CVEs) and the relationships between them, built up across every investigation rather than reset each time.\n- **Temporal decay** — a mathematical weighting that makes recent information matter more than old information, without discarding the old information entirely.\n- **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** — the standard way an AI agent (like Claude) discovers and calls external tools. This is the same mechanism used to let Claude Code itself query CausalOps's memory directly, for real, during this project's own verification work.\n\n## If You Only Read One Other Note\n\nIf the meeting is technical, read [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]]. If the meeting is about *how* the work was done (process, rigor, engineering judgment) rather than *what* was built, read [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]] and [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]] — those two notes are where the real engineering difficulty lived, arguably more so than in writing the new feature itself.\n\n## Note Index\n\n1. [[01 - What is CausalOps (Project Primer)]] — start here if you need the *entire* project explained from zero, including a worked example\n2. [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] — the five components in depth, with code\n3. [[03 - Supabase Schema, Migrations & Data Layer]] — the database side, with full SQL\n4. [[04 - The MCP Server and Protocol Bridge]] — how agents (including Claude Code itself) actually talk to the memory layer\n5. [[05 - Reconciling With Main — The Rebase Story]] — the hardest part of this PR, and why\n6. [[06 - Testing & Verification Methodology]] — how \"done\" was actually proven, not just claimed\n7. [[07 - Next Steps, Deferred Work & Career Takeaways]] — what's left, and how to talk about this work externally\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/01 - What is CausalOps (Project Primer).md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: reference\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, project-primer, onboarding]\n---\n\n# What is CausalOps? (Read This If You Know Nothing About the Project)\n\n> [!note] This note assumes zero prior context. If you already know what CausalOps is, skip to [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]].\n\n## The Problem CausalOps Solves\n\nLarge language models are very good at producing *convincing* explanations. They are equally good at producing convincing explanations that are **completely unsupported by evidence** — a phenomenon usually called \"hallucination,\" though in this context it's really an epistemology problem, not just a factual-accuracy problem.\n\nMost \"AI agent\" systems let an LLM do all three of these steps itself:\n1. Generate a hypothesis (\"this incident was caused by X\")\n2. Generate the supporting evidence\n3. Explain why the evidence proves the hypothesis\n\nThe result reads well — it has confident language, a plausible narrative, maybe even numbers in it — but it has no actual statistical foundation. The LLM is grading its own homework, and homework graded by the student who wrote it always passes.\n\nThis isn't a hypothetical concern for a cybersecurity tool. If an analyst trusts a fabricated causal claim (\"patching this vulnerability reduced attacks by 40%\") that was never actually tested against real data, they make real remediation decisions on a number that means nothing.\n\n## The Core Design Principle\n\n> *\"The LLM proposes hypotheses. Deterministic code falsifies them.\"*\n\nThis is CausalOps's one-sentence design philosophy, and it is enforced as a hard architectural boundary, not a guideline. Concretely, this boundary shows up as five separate rules, each backed by actual code:\n\n1. **The LLM never generates evidence rows.** `dataset_compiler.py` has an explicit guard: any evidence record tagged `source_type == \"synthetic\"` is silently dropped before it ever reaches the statistical estimator. There is no code path by which an LLM's output becomes a row in the dataset DoWhy estimates against.\n2. **A separate, deterministic evidence compiler** (`dataset_compiler.py`) ingests real SIEM logs, CVE records, and incident reports, and *only* that real data is used to test any hypothesis.\n3. **Statistical libraries compute the answer, not the LLM.** `DoWhy` (for the causal estimate) and `statsmodels` (for the p-value, computed independently via OLS regression) do the actual math. The LLM's role stops at proposing *which* variables might be causally related — it never gets to say what the effect size is.\n4. **A separate causal-discovery pass validates the LLM's proposed graph.** The LLM might hypothesize \"patching reduces lateral movement\" — but a PC-algorithm-based conditional-independence test (`causal_discovery.py`) checks that hypothesis against the *actual* evidence and **prunes any edge that isn't statistically supported**, regardless of how confident the LLM's proposal sounded.\n5. **If the evidence is too weak, the system refuses to produce a number.** Concretely: fewer than 50 complete treatment/outcome observations, fewer than 10 treated rows, fewer than 10 control rows, or no observed variation in treatment or outcome — any one of these triggers a refusal. The API returns exactly this instead of a fabricated result:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"method\": \"withheld:data_quality_gates\",\n  \"ate\": null,\n  \"confidence_interval\": null,\n  \"p_value\": null\n}\n```\n\n*This refusal-when-uncertain behavior is treated as a **feature**, not a bug — stated explicitly in the project's own documentation.* A system that always gives you an answer is less trustworthy than one that sometimes says \"the evidence doesn't support a conclusion yet,\" because the former has no way to distinguish a confident correct answer from a confident guess.\n\n## What \"CausalOps\" Actually Does, End to End — A Worked Example\n\nImagine a SOC analyst submits: *\"Suspected lateral movement via RDP in the finance segment — host FIN-042 shows unusual authentication patterns following a recent patch deployment.\"*\n\nHere is what happens, step by step, mapped to the ten pipeline stages CausalOps's own documentation names:\n\n| # | Stage | What happens with this specific example |\n|---|---|---|\n| 1 | **Decompose** | The orchestrator agent reads the incident and decides how many independent investigation \"tracks\" to spin up — e.g., one track for \"was this actually lateral movement,\" another for \"was the patch actually a factor.\" |\n| 2 | **Investigate** | Parent agents each spawn child agents with narrow, specific mandates — e.g. a child agent tasked purely with \"identify the fastest containment strategy\" writes a decision memo; another, tasked with \"name the telemetry needed to test causality,\" writes a different one. |\n| 3 | **Evaluate** | An evaluator agent (or, in the newer \"standard\" fast execution mode, a deterministic local scoring function) ranks the memos by relevance, reasoning quality, and constraint satisfaction. |\n| 4 | **Hypothesize** | A \"Causal Architect\" agent proposes a directed acyclic graph (DAG) — e.g., `Patch_Applied → Lateral_Movement`, with `Asset_Criticality` as a candidate confounder. |\n| 5 | **Compile Evidence** | The deterministic compiler pulls real evidence records — actual SIEM rows, actual CVE records — tagged with real `source_type` values, and normalizes them into a clean statistical dataset. Anything the LLM might have generated itself is rejected here, by rule 1 above. |\n| 6 | **Estimate** | If (and only if) the data quality gates pass, DoWhy computes an Average Treatment Effect (ATE) — e.g., \"applying the patch is associated with a −0.31 change in lateral-movement likelihood\" — with a genuine p-value from `statsmodels`, not a number the LLM invented. |\n| 7 | **Validate the Graph** | The PC-algorithm causal-discovery pass independently checks whether `Asset_Criticality` really behaves like a confounder in the actual data, or whether that edge should be pruned. |\n| 8 | **Reason** | A deterministic reasoning layer looks for anomalies in the whole picture and drafts recommended next actions — not another LLM call, by design (this is one of the project's own stated \"hard questions and answers\": *\"why isn't the reasoning layer another LLM?\"* — because a second LLM checking a first LLM's work is not independent verification, it's the same failure mode twice). |\n| 9 | **Learn** | A reinforcement-learning loop updates policy priors — e.g., if \"Evidence & Causal Measurement Analyst\" personas have historically produced higher-quality memos for RDP-related incidents, that gets reflected in future agent configuration for similar incidents. |\n| 10 | **Remember** | The completed investigation becomes part of a persistent 5-dimensional knowledge graph *(a separate, pre-existing system — see the callout below)*. |\n\n**This PR's contribution sits conceptually alongside steps 1 and 10**: the new memory layer retrieves relevant *past* investigations (like this exact FIN-042 example, if a similar one existed) *before* step 1 even begins, and persists the finished investigation for future retrieval *after* step 9 completes — regardless of whether the fast or full pipeline was used. See [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for the precise mechanics.\n\n> [!warning] Two different \"memory\" systems exist in this codebase — don't confuse them.\n> - The **5D Spatiotemporal Knowledge Graph** (`graph_5d.py`) already existed before this PR. It's a `(subject, predicate, object, time, location)` graph that powers reinforcement learning, historical replay, and visualization *within* the artifacts of investigations that have run through this system, primarily for the RL/policy-learning loop.\n> - The **Persistent Semantic Memory Layer** (this PR's subject) is new, and lives in Supabase rather than the local SQLite/graph database. It works *across* runs in a way the 5D graph alone was never designed for — it's what lets the system recognize \"this looks like the incident from three weeks ago\" using semantic (meaning-based) similarity search, not just structural graph traversal.\n> See [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for full detail on the new system, and how the two systems relate.\n\n## Why \"Agent Swarm,\" Not \"One Agent\" — And Why It Evolves\n\nCausalOps deliberately uses a *hierarchy* of specialized agents rather than one large LLM call answering everything at once:\n\n```\nOrchestrator (decomposes the incident)\n   ├── Parent Agent 1 (e.g. \"Rapid SOC Triage Lead\")\n   │      ├── Child Agent 1a (e.g. \"Containment & Blast Radius Analyst\")\n   │      └── Child Agent 1b (e.g. \"Evidence & Causal Measurement Analyst\")\n   └── Parent Agent 2 (if the orchestrator decided a second track was warranted)\n          └── Child Agent 2a\n```\n\nEach child agent writes exactly one decision memo, from one narrow perspective. The evaluator then ranks these memos rather than trusting any single agent's confidence in its own answer — a form of the same \"don't let something grade its own homework\" principle that governs evidence, applied to agent output itself.\n\n**Agents also evolve, and this is not an LLM-driven process either.** A deterministic **steady-state island evolutionary algorithm** (tournament selection, crossover, bounded mutation, periodic migration between \"islands\" of agent configurations) tunes each agent's policy — traits like `evidence_weight`, `causal_focus`, `temporal_awareness`, `risk_aversion`, `coordination` — across runs. Reinforcement learning (a model-based value-iteration approach, computing a Stackelberg-style leader/follower response between parent and child policy tiers) further refines these policies based on how well past investigations' strategies actually performed, feeding a shared \"meta-prior\" back down into future agent configurations. None of this tuning is done by asking an LLM \"how should agents behave differently\" — it's computed.\n\n## The Execution Path That Actually Runs in Production — A Detail Worth Getting Right\n\nThere are two versions of the coordination logic in this codebase, and confusing them is a common and costly mistake for anyone new to the project:\n\n- **`src/graph.py`** — a LangGraph state-graph implementation. **This is reference-only.** Its own module docstring explicitly says it is deprecated for execution. It's useful for understanding the conceptual topology of the pipeline, but nothing in production actually runs through it.\n- **`src/coordinator/runner.py::execute_run()`** — the **real** execution path: an async state machine that persists progress to SQLite (`data/runs.db`) between every single phase, so a run's state survives a process restart mid-investigation.\n\nThis distinction mattered directly for the memory-layer work: the new `memory_retrieve`/`memory_write` phases were added to `coordinator/runner.py`, not `graph.py` — adding them only to the reference implementation would have produced code that looked correct in review but did nothing in the actual running system.\n\n## The Technology Stack, With the \"Why\" Behind Each Choice\n\n| Layer | Technology | Why this, specifically |\n|---|---|---|\n| Chat LLM | NVIDIA Nemotron (primary) → Gemini (fallback) → Azure OpenAI (final fallback) | A three-tier fallback chain, checked in `src/llm.py`'s `get_llm()` function in priority order — if the primary provider's key isn't set, it silently falls through, so the system degrades gracefully rather than hard-failing on a single provider outage |\n| Causal inference | DoWhy + statsmodels | DoWhy gives a principled causal-inference framework (identification, estimation, refutation); statsmodels is used *independently* to compute the p-value via OLS, so the p-value isn't just DoWhy's own internal number — it's a second, separately-computed statistic |\n| Causal discovery | PC algorithm (conditional independence testing) | A well-established, non-LLM algorithm for inferring which edges in a proposed causal graph are actually statistically defensible given the data |\n| Event bus | Kafka (via Redpanda) | Decouples the coordinator from worker processes, allowing horizontal scaling of the \"spawn\" workload (dispatching parent/child agent tasks) independently of the API |\n| Run persistence | SQLite (`data/runs.db`) | Chosen deliberately for local/single-node deployments; the codebase's own `RunStore`/`WorkerExecutor` interfaces are designed to allow a future swap to Redis/Postgres without changing calling code |\n| **Memory layer (this PR)** | **Supabase (Postgres + pgvector) + Gemini embeddings + standalone MCP server** | See [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] for the full rationale — briefly, Postgres+pgvector avoids introducing an entirely separate vector-database technology when a well-understood relational database extension does the job |\n| Frontend | React 19 + TanStack Start | A modern, server-side-rendering-capable React framework |\n| Backend | FastAPI | Async-native Python web framework, matching the async-throughout design of the coordinator |\n\n## A Short Glossary (For Anyone New to This Domain)\n\n- **ATE (Average Treatment Effect)** — the statistical estimate of how much a \"treatment\" (e.g., applying a patch) causally affects an \"outcome\" (e.g., likelihood of lateral movement), as opposed to a mere correlation.\n- **DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)** — a graph with directional edges and no cycles, used here to represent a hypothesized causal structure (X causes Y, Y causes Z, etc., with no loops).\n- **Confounder** — a variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, and which — if not accounted for — can make an estimate misleadingly attribute an effect to the treatment that's actually caused by the confounder.\n- **Refutation test** — a check DoWhy runs to see whether its own estimate holds up under perturbation (e.g., adding a random common cause, or subsetting the data) — a sanity check on the estimate itself, not just on whether one was produced.\n- **DoWhy** — the open-source causal-inference Python library CausalOps uses for identification, estimation, and refutation.\n- **MITRE ATT&CK technique ID** — a standardized identifier (like `T1021.001`, \"Remote Desktop Protocol\") for a specific adversary tactic, from the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base — the industry-standard taxonomy this project uses to tag techniques.\n\n## Where to Go Next\n\nNow that you know what CausalOps *is* and how a single incident flows through it end to end, [[02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component]] explains exactly what this PR added to it — with code.\n"}`
- `mcp__jarvis__vault_write` — `{"path":"60_Claude/40_Project_Briefs/CausalOps/Memory Layer PR Summary/02 - The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component.md","content":"---\ntype: project\nstatus: complete\ncreated: 2026-07-09\ntags: [causalops, memory-layer, architecture, implementation]\n---\n\n# The Persistent Memory Layer, Component by Component\n\n> [!info] This is the deep-dive technical note. If you need the short version first, read [[00 - Executive Summary (Meeting Prep)]].\n\nThe roadmap asked for five things. All five are implemented, tested, and verified live.
